articles.title: Automating beauty: Detecting facial changes in platform beauty filters
articles.authors: Julia Coffey, Kiah Hawker, Amy Dobson, Niamh White, Rosalind Gill, Akane Kanai
articles.abstract: Beauty filters have become everyday instruments in digital media’s visual and participatory cultures. Such filters use AR (augmented reality) and AI (artificial intelligence) technologies and apply a digital mask over a user’s face and automate ‘corrections’ to a user’s face, most commonly skin smoothing, balancing features such as noses and eyes, and enhancing lips, in accordance with dominant racialised beauty expectations. In this article, we provide an overview of the evolution of AR and AI automation processes that are embedded in contemporary filters used in TikTok and Instagram and explore how filters and beauty expectations are experienced and navigated by young people. We found young people are highly suspicious of the automated changes filters can make to their faces ‘without asking’, and felt platforms should ‘own up’ to precisely how their faces are being changed. They were also critical of how filters repeat and reinforce existing gendered and racialised beauty norms, but found these norms harder to challenge when a supposedly ‘objective’ measure of beauty was reinscribed through the technology: ‘the filter tells you what your flaws are’. We situate these technologies as enabling the automation of ‘beauty’ and examine its impacts for prevailing gendered and racialised beauty norms and inequalities.

articles.title: Just one more swipe: Why short-form feeds are hard to stop
articles.authors: Lasse Juel Larsen
articles.abstract: This article develops a psycho-systemic theory of withheld closure to explain why short-form feeds such as TikTok, Reels, and Shorts are difficult to stop. It uses the concept as a critical lens on digital culture. An analytic vignette anchors a constellational synthesis across four interacting dimensions: cognition, communication, computation, and culture. The four Cs map the terrain, while five theoretical lenses specify distinct forms of non-closure within or across it. Bluma Zeigarnik chiefly illuminates cognitive unfinishedness; Johan Asplund, experienced responsiveness in communication; and Alan Turing, procedural non-termination in computation. Niklas Luhmann bridges communication and computation by showing how selections become conditions for further operations, while Jacques Derrida bridges media-textual communication and culture through semantic deferral. Critical media scholarship further specifies culture through normalization, metrics, and value. Together, these lenses reveal a psycho-systemic coupling: the user is held in tension between an orientation toward continuation and an orientation toward closure, whether through completion or disengagement, while the feed is organized around continuation. Withheld closure names this relation, not a user trait, textual device, or interface feature. At the session level, even clips that end cleanly can lead directly to a successor, making nextness the locally supported default. Methodologically, this article adopts a stance of againstness: it refuses single-register monopolies (neural-only, design-only, trait-only, or culture-only). Instead, it theorizes how psychic orientation and systemic organization couple at the session level. This approach treats theory as a revisable working model that highlights key differences without claiming finality. Thus, withheld closure encapsulates a relation in which continuation means staying in motion and the end is deferred. In feeds shaped by nextness, stopping becomes an act of digital resistance.

articles.title: Algorithmic commonsense knowledge and everyday TikTok practices: An ethnomethodological inquiry
articles.authors: Chia-Rong Tsao
articles.abstract: This study employs ethnomethodology to examine how TikTok users sustain and reconstruct algorithmic “commonsense knowledge” in everyday practices. Unlike previous research on algorithm awareness, algorithmic imaginaries, or folk theories of algorithms, this study analyzes how users’ algorithmic commonsense knowledge operates as an ongoing practical accomplishment. Based on 26 in-depth interviews with Taiwanese university students, I demonstrate that algorithmic commonsense knowledge functions through background expectancies and practical reasoning in users’ interactions with TikTok’s algorithmic system. The findings reveal how algorithmic power relations become naturalized through heterogeneous assemblages of material interfaces, user practices, and mutual accountability between users and algorithmic systems.

articles.title: Heroic construction and messianic authoritarianism: A ludonarrative analysis of Mass Effect 3
articles.authors: Pablo Romero-Medina, Júlia Vilasís-Pamos
articles.abstract: This article presents a ludonarrative analysis of the video game Mass Effect 3 through Thomas Carlyle’s Great Man Theory. Starting from a conception of the video game as a cultural product, it explores the ways in which the work constructs its protagonist, Shepard, as an exceptional figure whose individual will determine the political destiny of the galaxy. By examining formal elements, gameplay mechanics, and paratexts, it investigates how the ludonarrative structure reproduces authoritarian, hierarchical, and meritocratic models of leadership. The study identifies the presence of ideological imaginaries that legitimize strong authority figures as responses to contexts of crisis, in line with contemporary neoconservative and alt-right discourses. Far from offering a neutral experience, the game articulates a rhetoric that naturalizes the centrality of the lone hero, reinforcing individualistic representations of power and contributing to the normalization of personalist authority structures.

articles.title: Human or Not? Prior Knowledge, Recognition of Virtual Identity, and Neural and Subjective Responses to a Hyperrealistic Virtual Influencer
articles.authors: Heeran Lee, Yoo-Kyoung Seock
articles.abstract: Despite the growing popularity of virtual social media influencers (VIs), little is known about how knowledge and recognition of a VI’s virtual identity are associated with neural and subjective responses. We investigated whether prior knowledge of virtual identity, recognition during viewing, or remaining unaware was associated with differences in brain activity and subjective evaluations. Twenty female college students viewed a 1-minute silent video featuring a hyperrealistic Korean virtual influencer while electroencephalographic (EEG) activity was recorded. Subsequently, participants completed subjective evaluations and retrospectively reported prior knowledge or recognition of the influencer’s virtual identity. Exploratory analyses compared EEG changes from eyes-closed rest and five subjective evaluation composite scores across the three groups, with correction for multiple comparisons. After correction for multiple comparisons, neither the EEG analyses nor the subjective composite analyses yielded statistically significant group differences. Descriptive means varied across groups, but these imprecisely estimated patterns did not establish group differences. The findings underscore the methodological importance of distinguishing prior knowledge from recognition during viewing. Computers Are Social Actors and Uncanny Valley perspectives generate hypotheses for future time-resolved studies rather than mechanisms demonstrated by the present data.

articles.title: Symptom-Level Comorbidity Patterns Between Depression and Internet Gaming Disorder Among Adolescents: Evidence from Longitudinal Network Analysis with Gender Considerations
articles.authors: Shiyun Chen, Yue Zhao, Xinli Chi, Shimin Zhu
articles.abstract: Adolescence is a period with an increased risk for the co-occurrence of depression and Internet gaming disorder (IGD), yet we still know little about how specific symptoms of these two conditions influence each other over time. In this study, we applied cross-lagged panel network analysis to two-wave data from a community sample of 538 adolescents (Mean age = 12.51 years; 53.7 percent female). Potential gender differences in the network structure were examined. In the overall sample and in both gender groups, depressive symptoms consistently predicted later gaming-related problems, whereas no reverse cross-disorder pathways were retained. In particular, suicidal ideation and psychomotor symptoms emerged as bridge symptoms linking depression and IGD, while sleep problems showed moderate outgoing expected influence in the overall symptom network. While boys and girls showed broadly similar patterns, some differences emerged in how specific symptoms were connected and which symptoms were most influential. These findings clarify the longitudinal symptom-level associations between depression and IGD in adolescents, suggesting that addressing key depressive symptoms may help reduce the risk of later IGD.

articles.title: Knowing You Seeing Me: The Role of Visual Contact During Video-Conferencing for Emotion Recognition and Mimicry
articles.authors: Michal Olszanowski, Aleksandra Fortuńska, Natalia Frankowska
articles.abstract: This study investigated how asymmetrical visual access in video-conferencing—specifically sender and receiver camera status—affects emotion recognition and facial mimicry. Ninety-one participants viewed bimodal (facial-vocal) or vocal-only displays of four emotions (anger, disgust, sadness, and happiness) while their own camera was either on or off. Recognition accuracy, intensity ratings, and facial muscle activity electromyography (EMG) were recorded. Results revealed that bimodal displays significantly enhanced recognition accuracy and perceived intensity compared with vocal-only signals, except for sadness. Emotional mimicry was most pronounced for affiliative displays (happiness and sadness) and was significantly stronger in the bimodal condition. Exploratory analyses suggested that the awareness of being observed (self-camera on) intensified smile-like reactions and improved the recognition of sadness. These findings suggest that mutual visibility facilitates emotion recognition and affiliative mimicry. The self-camera may function as a cue for public self-awareness, possibly sharpening sensitivity to an interlocutor’s emotional signals. This research highlights the importance of multimodal communication in sustaining interpersonal synchronization during remote interactions.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and journalism in Ibero-America: A comparative study of perceptions, practices and challenges
articles.authors: Paulo Nuno Vicente, Sara Pérez-Seijo, Suzana Barbosa
articles.abstract: This article explores the perceptions, practices, challenges and opportunities associated with the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in journalistic practice within the Ibero-American context. Drawing on an original quantitative comparative study conducted in Portugal, Spain and Brazil, the research investigates how professional journalists understand, engage with and respond to the integration of AI-driven tools in newsrooms. Based on survey data from 271 journalists, the findings reveal widespread but predominantly basic knowledge of AI, general curiosity and cautious optimism regarding its implementation, and notable concern about its impact on professional ethics, job security, and editorial transparency. The study highlights significant variations across countries in the use of AI applications. Key challenges identified include the absence of formal editorial guidelines, limited training opportunities and a lack of transparency in the use of AI-generated content. The research underscores the urgent need for institutional strategies that ensure responsible AI integration, safeguard journalistic standards and support professional development.

articles.title: Trending by design: How algorithmic activists amplified and recalibrated an elite anti-Ukrainian campaign on X
articles.authors: Piotr Marczyński
articles.abstract: The ability of far-right actors to manipulate social media traffic sparks concerns over the quality of public discourse. Although the scholarship on far-right digital activism has established its role in aiding elite communication, we know little about mechanisms through which such campaigns are amplified and recalibrated in the process. This article addresses this gap through the lens of algorithmic activism, investigating how digital activists leveraged platform features to amplify and recalibrate the elite-initiated campaign #StopUkrainizacjiPolski on X. Combining descriptive statistics, social network analysis and critical discourse analysis, we examine 130,788 posts from February 2022 to September 2024. Findings demonstrate that a small group of accounts amplified the hashtag by hijacking the X trending board while recalibrating campaign objectives via indexical linkages to other hashtags, invoking instrumental pacifism, historical grievances, and antisemitic conspiracy theories. The study elucidates how platform affordances shape how digital activists engage in elite campaigns with implications for the reach and form of exclusionary discourse.

articles.title: The Ludic Library: Magic, Cosmology, and Enchantment in The Elder Scrolls In-Game Book Corpus
articles.authors: Maelaynayn El Baida
articles.abstract: Critics of ludic magic have long diagnosed game magic systems as mechanistically unenchanting: rational, quantifiable, and drained of wonder. These critiques target mechanics and largely ignore the textual layer. This paper examines that layer directly. Applying Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling and a keyword-dictionary operationalization of Faivre's four criteria of enchantment to a corpus of 710 Elder Scrolls in-game books (∼590,000 words), I map the distribution and intensity of enchanted cosmological content across the franchise's textual archive. Results identify a stratified structure: a dominant cosmological cluster anchored by Daedric theology and divine hierarchy scores highest on Imagination and Mediations and Correspondences; a smaller mythological cluster scores highest on Living Nature and Transmutation; a magic-instruction cluster scores high on Living Nature alone, reproducing at the textual level the mechanistic flatness critics attribute to the mechanics. I propose the ludic library as a distinct enchantment mechanism that proceduralist frameworks systematically undercount.

articles.title: Digital Cartographies of Exclusion: Mapping Inequality in Global Virtual Flight Simulation
articles.authors: S Anas Ahmad
articles.abstract: Formally open digital worlds can remain unevenly inhabited. This article examines Virtual Air Traffic Simulation Network, a global volunteer flight-simulation network, through postcolonial game studies and infrastructure scholarship, asking how infrastructural and historical conditions may shape participation and visibility. It combines Navigraph survey data, StatSim records from four matched 2025 routine-network windows and event geography, including Cross the Pond, and reflexive thematic analysis of asynchronous interviews with 15 participants across six regional contexts. Results show recurrent concentrations of simulated flight activity, volunteer air traffic control, and organized attention in Europe, while South Asia remains comparatively sparse; Dubai complicates a simple Global North/Global South binary. Survey comparisons caution against treating sparse activity as evidence of weak interest. Interviews identify recursive visibility, human infrastructure, route path dependence, and the costs of concentration as participant-reported mechanisms. The article conceptualizes these patterns as infrastructural inheritances: unevenly accumulated aviation resources translated into digital participation without implying direct historical determination.

articles.title: Thanato-Sensitive Design in Digital Games: A Scoping Review and Comparative Analysis of Emotional and Narrative Approaches to Death, Grief, and Memory
articles.authors: Mariana Silva Cabral, Ana Carla Amaro
articles.abstract: In most digital games, death sanctions failed play and is undone by retrying. Some titles, however, design it as a loss with emotional, narrative, and ethical weight. A PRISMA-ScR-compliant scoping review of 17 studies (2020–2025) shows that conceptual and single-case qualitative work predominates, and design-led research is scarce. A framework derived from the review and comprising five dimensions—Representation of Death, Narrative and Memory Structure, Player Positioning, Mechanics and Pacing, and Instrumentalization and Restraint—guided a comparative analysis of Spiritfarer , GRIS , OMORI , and What Remains of Edith Finch. Each game achieves a thanato-sensitive treatment of death by its own formal means, and all four share a coherent alignment across the five dimensions and a withdrawal of the player's control over whether death occurs. A working definition of thanato-sensitive design, centered on ethical orientation and design coherence, is proposed.

articles.title: At what cost? Unintended lateral effects of persuasive messages linking liked and disliked concepts
articles.authors: Shannon M Cruz, Yanitza A Cruz Crespo, David M Keating
articles.abstract: Persuasive campaigns often rely on drawing connections between concepts evaluated in opposing ways. Campaigns might encourage adoption of disliked behaviors by linking them to positive health outcomes, for example, or discourage support for popular policies by revealing their negative environmental consequences. These arguments are often effective in changing targeted attitudes, but we show experimentally (N = 1,002) that they can also lead to undesirable effects on other, related (i.e., lateral) attitudes. Specifically, we found that linking a negatively evaluated object (flies) to a positively evaluated one (pollinators, butterflies) led to positive direct attitude change at the expense of negative lateral attitude change. Although the cognitive mechanisms that account for this finding cannot be observed directly, we suggest that these effects may arise as people strive to resolve the cognitive inconsistencies such messages generate while maintaining accurate attitudes. Lateral attitude effects merit greater consideration in persuasion theory and campaign design.

articles.title: GenAI governance maturity and divergent use pathways at work: sanctioned assimilation depth and shadow use
articles.authors: Stanley Y. B. Huang
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines how employee-perceived generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) governance maturity relates to approved enterprise use and unauthorized public-tool use in data-sensitive work. Design/methodology/approach A two-wave survey of 750 knowledge workers in Taiwan was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Additional checks examine same-occasion measurement, available controls, sector sensitivity and an alternative assimilation-to-shadow-use path. Findings regulatory pressure and internal guideline salience were positively associated with governance maturity. Governance maturity was positively related to safe-to-use climate and perceived data exposure risk. The former was associated with sanctioned assimilation depth and task performance; the latter was negatively associated with shadow GenAI Use, which was positively related to employee creativity. These associations suggest a tension between reliable sanctioned performance and risk-laden exploration. Originality/value Sanctioned assimilation depth and shadow GenAI use are distinct appropriation modes, not opposite ends of one use continuum. Integrating institutional and socio-technical perspectives explains how governance differentiates the conditions attached to approved and unapproved channels without assuming that consumer-led workplace technology use is new.

articles.title: Understanding user agency and structural conditions in information system implementation: a study in industrial maintenance
articles.authors: Heini Ikävalko, Miia Martinsuo, Elviira Saarelma
articles.abstract: Purpose Users within the same organization may enact the same digital information system differently, creating diverse requirements and challenges for implementation. It is essential to view information system implementation as a process shaped by individuals' capacity to act within organizational structures, that is, through their agency. This study explores the manifestation of user agency and its associated structural conditions in information system implementation. Design/methodology/approach We examined users' experiences of information system implementation in two industrial companies' maintenance operations, through an interpretive qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews. Findings The study identifies four types of agency, namely eligible, estranged, skilled and motivated, and shows ways in which structural conditions of work design, social relationships and practices and situated individual resources in information system users' work both enable and hinder user's capacity to act during information system implementation. Practical implications The identified agency types can help managers in tailoring information system implementation support. Acknowledging work design, collaborative practices and situated resources enhances users' capacity to act with the new system. Originality/value This study contributes by introducing a typology of user agency in information system implementation: it provides a fine-grained lens to explain why users facing the same information system enact it differently and extends enactment-oriented information system research on human agency. Showing how agency is conditioned by work design, social relationships and practices and situated individual resources in users' unique work conditions, it addresses agency as part of the social and structural dynamics of information system implementation.

articles.title: The challenge of AI dependence: exploring its impact on cognitive autonomy and elaboration in creative performance
articles.authors: Yanyang Ma, Kerun Li, Yulei Liu
articles.abstract: Purpose As artificial intelligence advances and its application scenarios continue to expand, human–artificial intelligence interaction grows increasingly close. While artificial intelligence brings convenience, it also raises concerns that it may weaken users' cognitive autonomy. To investigate this issue. This study aims to explore the composition of AI dependence and its impact on cognitive autonomy and specific aspects of creative performance. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on cognitive evaluation theory and the elaboration likelihood model to construct a dual-pathway model with instrumental dependence and affective dependence as core variables. The model explains the formation mechanisms of the two types of artificial intelligence dependence and their differential effects on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily examines their potential role in the elaboration dimension of creative performance. A two-stage mixed-method design was employed to test the model. Findings Study 1 found that perceived trust mainly had a positive effect on instrumental dependence. Different dimensions of interactivity differentially affected affective dependence and cognitive autonomy. Mediation analysis further confirmed the core mediating role of Dependence. Study 2, a small-sample exploratory experiment, re-tested selected hypotheses and found a possible negative effect of instrumental dependence on the elaboration dimension of creative performance. Research limitations/implications The main theoretical contribution of this study lies in revealing the dual-pathway formation mechanisms of artificial intelligence dependence and the reshaping effects of different types of dependence on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily explores the potential effects of dependence on elaboration performance. Originality/value The dual-pathway dependence model constructed in this study offers practical implications for understanding how long-term use of artificial intelligence affects cognitive autonomy.

articles.title: Understanding the enacted behaviors of university students susceptible to cybersecurity risks: a community of practice perspective
articles.authors: Maharazu Kasim, Anup Shrestha, Samuel C. Avemaria Utulu
articles.abstract: Purpose Organizations carry out an ethical hacking approach to combat cybersecurity challenges, focusing on the technical aspects of cybersecurity vulnerabilities. This practice persists despite evidence that shows that human-enacted cybersecurity vulnerabilities constitute a significant threat to organizational cybersecurity. To address this challenge, we propose a socio-ethical hacking framework to deal with cybersecurity vulnerabilities in organizations. This framework shows how these behaviors are embedded in and reinforced through the everyday practices of organizational actors. Design/methodology/approach We adopted an interpretive case study research method using the community of practice (CoP) theory as the theoretical lens and university undergraduate students as the study context. Research data were collected through interviews and participatory observation. Findings The study identified how the social structure of undergraduate students shapes the enactment of behaviors that constitute cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Organizational actors jointly create social behaviors and actions that make organizations vulnerable to cybersecurity challenges. Practical implications Using this study, organizations can combine both technical ethical hacking and social ethical hacking practices to detect technical and behavioral vulnerabilities that expose their organization to cyber security threats. Social implications Organizations develop new insights on how to detect taken-for-granted enacted vulnerabilities that can surpass the best cyber security protocols put in place. Using the CoP theory, this study has established the relevance of social factors and how they can enhance understanding human vulnerability, particularly behaviors vulnerable to cybersecurity threats. Originality/value While there are numerous studies looking at the human factor in cybersecurity, there is little evidence of studies showing how these behaviors are enacted and experienced as taken-for-granted actions within their social contexts. This study enhanced studies in the human vulnerability research stream particularly as they relate to how social structure of organizational actors lead to the enactment of behaviors susceptible to a cybersecurity threat.

articles.title: Augmentation or automation? A dual-path model of GenAI usage motivations and employee creativity
articles.authors: Yujie Shi, Jiang Xu, Jih-Yu Mao, Minya Xu
articles.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can both enhance and constrain employee creativity, yet the mechanisms underlying these divergent effects remain unclear. This study examines how augmentation and automation motivations for GenAI usage shape employee creativity through distinct knowledge-processing mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on dual-process theory and self-regulation theory, we distinguish augmentation and automation motivations for GenAI usage and propose distinct cognitive mechanisms linking them to creativity. We test the hypotheses using a multi-wave, multi-source field survey and a scenario-based experiment. Findings Augmentation motivation is positively associated with employee creativity through knowledge integration, whereas automation motivation is negatively related to creativity through knowledge dependence. Conscientiousness strengthens the positive indirect effect of augmentation motivation and attenuates the negative indirect effect of automation motivation on employee creativity. Research limitations/implications Augmentation and automation motivations may coexist and vary across tasks and use episodes. Future research could explore these dynamics, examine how other individual differences shape their effects, and assess whether the consequences of GenAI dependence vary across work contexts. Practical implications Organizations should encourage employees to use GenAI to generate and develop ideas rather than replace their own judgment. Training could help employees critically assess AI-generated suggestions and combine them with their own knowledge. Originality/value This research shifts attention from how much employees use GenAI to why they use it. By distinguishing augmentation and automation motivations, it explains when and why GenAI can enhance or constrain employee creativity through distinct knowledge-processing mechanisms.

articles.title: Won’t somebody please think of practitioners? Understanding practitioner engagement with academic information systems research
articles.authors: Cathal Doyle, Qianyi Li, Kristijan Mirkovski, Paul Benjamin Lowry
articles.abstract: Purpose This paper examines why practitioner engagement with academic Information Systems (IS) research remains limited despite the long-standing rigour-relevance debate. It reframes the issue as a knowledge adoption and translation problem by explaining how practitioners recognise, access, and use academic research in work practice. Design/methodology/approach Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 315 IS practitioners, primarily from the UK and the US, with a small component from New Zealand. The research model was tested using partial least squares path modelling. Bootstrapped mediation analysis examined indirect effects, and multivariate analysis of variance with follow-up analyses of variance assessed differences. Findings Innovation autonomy positively affected perceived content relevance, but not perceived communication relevance, suggesting that practitioner discretion helps practitioners recognise substantive value but does not resolve communication barriers embedded in academic research artefacts. Perceived communication relevance increased access intention to informal sources. In contrast, perceived content relevance increased access intention to both formal and informal sources, indicating that strong substantive relevance generates complementary rather than substitutive access pathways. Access to both informal and formal sources increased research engagement behaviour. Practical implications IS researchers should tailor dissemination to practitioner profiles and use clearer translational formats. IS journals should strengthen their mechanisms for practitioner-facing publications beyond conventional statements of practical implications. Originality/value The paper offers a practitioner-centred, empirically tested process model showing that engagement depends on perceived value, communication, and access pathways, rather than on relevance alone. The staged structure is used as a theoretical framework, while the empirical findings are interpreted as cross-sectional associations.

articles.title: Actualizing the external enablement of generative artificial intelligence: evidence from software new ventures
articles.authors: Jiyoung Kim, Joaquin Cestino, Tim Luca Greiner, Simon Hund
articles.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools have been argued to enable entrepreneurial endeavors. Employing the external enablement framework, we examine how, if at all, the venture-level benefits offered by GenAI tools – termed GenAI enablement – are actualized in new ventures. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a qualitative design with 10 entrepreneurs in the software industry and five AI-entrepreneurship experts, we capture instances where entrepreneurs succeed or fail to capitalize on GenAI enablement and analyze the mechanisms underlying these different pathways. Findings Our findings lead to a model that outlines the actualization pathways of GenAI enablement, emphasizing that the properties of enablement (i.e. opacity, agency-intensity and outcome-variability) – beyond the mere availability of GenAI enablement – are crucial in explaining whether and how enablement is actualized. Research limitations/implications Given the small sample and specific research context during the early diffusion of GenAI, our findings warrant further examination across industries, countries and stages of technological diffusion. Future research could test and extend our model by examining the roles of outcome-variability and insufficient enablement in determining whether and how GenAI enablement is actualized, as well as how its actualization relates to venture performance. Originality/value Our study lays the groundwork for further theoretical and empirical investigation into the enabling influence of GenAI in entrepreneurship and business research, and provides conceptual refinements to the external enablement framework.

articles.title: Promotion or substitution? The effect of AI assistants on physician performance in online healthcare platforms
articles.authors: Weicheng Wang, Shaoqi Zhang, Min Zhang, Xitong Guo
articles.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping healthcare delivery. Physician-specific AI assistants, trained on individual physicians’ medical data, now provide personalized medical advice on online healthcare platforms. While AI assistants improve the availability of physician expertise, they may substitute for cognitive tasks traditionally undertaken by physicians. Despite this tension, few studies have examined how AI assistants affect physician performance. This study aims to examine the causal impact of introducing AI assistants on physician consultation volume and how physicians’ existing resource configurations shape this impact. Design/methodology/approach This study leveraged the introduction of AI assistants on a leading online healthcare platform to establish a quasi-natural experimental setting. We constructed a panel dataset covering 3,668 physicians and employed a difference-in-differences model to identify the causal effect of AI assistants on physician performance. Findings The results suggest that the introduction of AI assistants significantly improves physician performance, with physicians experiencing a 3.6% increase in consultation volume. Moderation analyses reveal that the positive effect is weaker for high-reputation physicians and those with broader knowledge. Further heterogeneity analysis shows that the effect is invariant to physician gender but more pronounced among physicians in non-first-tier cities. Originality/value This study provides causal evidence of the impact of AI assistants on individual performance in an online healthcare setting. It further reveals how physicians’ existing resource configurations shape AI’s impact from a resource-based view and offers suggestive evidence on its promotion and substitution pathways.

articles.title: Softening the spring: Sensitization of transient media effects through repeated exposure over time
articles.authors: Yuqian Ni, Joshua Baldwin, Allan D Tate, Michael D Schmidt, Kyle Johnsen, Sun Joo (Grace) Ahn
articles.abstract: Existing longitudinal media effects research often emphasizes overall trends in behavioral or attitudinal changes, while overlooking fluctuations that occur before and after each exposure instance. This oversight can obscure the mechanisms underlying longitudinal media effects, particularly how they accumulate from successive short-term effects. We hypothesized a sensitization process where a single media exposure induces a transient change in behavior followed by a rapid decay, while repeated exposure gradually strengthen the magnitude of transient effects and make them more sustained. We tested this hypothesis by analyzing continuously recorded behavioral data collected via wearable sensors over 6 months. During this period, children repeatedly interacted with an integrated system of media technology designed to promote physical activity (PA). Data partially supported the hypothesized sensitization process. Children’s PA showed a transient increase following single exposures. Moreover, although the transient effect did not become more sustained over time, it grew in magnitude with repeated exposure.

articles.title: “I Think of Myself as Other People's AI”: Robotomorphy, Self-Robotization, and AI's Influence on Human–Human Intimacy
articles.authors: Bibo Lin, Jindong Leo-Liu, Liang Cao, Shuyi Pan
articles.abstract: Drawing on robotomorphy, an approach that people attribute robotic features to humans, this study examines how robotomorphic experiences in the human–artificial intelligence (AI) intimacy context are interpreted and thereby shape people's understanding of themselves and human–human intimacy. Based on semistructured interviews with 29 users who have been in intimate relationships with AI, the findings show that the AI-as-a-benchmark process (normative) has been more widely reported than the AI-as-a-mirror process (descriptive). Users actively reflected on the capabilities of humans and AI without necessarily blurring the ontological boundaries between them, and ultimately formed new expectations for themselves and their human partners in intimate relationships. We proposed the term “self-robotization” to describe how people are self-encouraged to act like an AI.

articles.title: A History of Childhood Maltreatment and Marital Functioning: A Dyadic Latent Profile Analysis
articles.authors: Osnat Zamir, Ohad Szepsenwol, Ruby Charak, Inga Schalinski, Dana Lassri, Jessica Borelli
articles.abstract: A history of childhood maltreatment (CM) is a critical risk factor for marital challenges, but dyadic patterns of CM and relationship dynamics remain underexplored. This study utilized dyadic latent profile analysis (LPA) to identify distinct couple profiles based on both partners’ CM severity and marital functioning, focusing on marital quality, positive communication, and perceived partner responsiveness. The study further examined whether these profiles differ in posttraumatic stress and depressive symptoms. A sample of 393 mixed-sex Israeli married couples completed standardized self-report measures. LPA revealed four profiles: Low-Risk High-Functioning (LRHF; 85%), Moderate-Risk Distressed Couples (MRDC; 9.2%), High-Risk Wives Low-Functioning (HRWLF; 3.5%), and High-Risk Men Resilient Couples (HRMRC; 2.3%). Women in the HRWLF and men in the MRDC profiles, both with higher-than-average CM severity and lower marital functioning, reported higher levels of psychological symptoms. Conversely, women in the HRMRC profile, despite elevated CM severity, showed marital functioning similar to women in the LRHF group and reported the lowest psychological distress. This study advances the understanding of risk and resilience of couples in the context of CM, emphasizing the interplay between each partner’s CM severity, marital dynamics, especially perceived partner responsiveness, and gender. The findings highlight the need for trauma-informed, gender-sensitive couple interventions that strengthen relational functioning to buffer the psychological impact of CM history.

articles.title: A Mixed-Method Examination of Parents’ Alcohol Harm-Reduction Messages to Their Emerging Adult Children
articles.authors: Lucy E. Napper, Diana S. Ebersole, Gabrielle Maramag, Laura C. Wolter, Gavin Q. Fox
articles.abstract: Emerging adults often receive parental advice on drinking safely; however, research examining the content of these harm-reduction conversations from parents’ perspectives remains limited. With emerging adulthood as a theoretical framework for contextualizing young adults’ experiences, this study explores the nature of advice U.S. parents provide to their emerging adult children (ages 18 to 25) regarding alcohol use. A sample of parents of emerging adults ( N = 627) completed an online survey describing their harm-reduction conversations. Thematic analysis of responses revealed five major categories: specific protective behavioral strategies, independent decision-making advice, ambiguous advice, warning-based messages, and advice conveying approval. Additionally, two new themes emerged: help-seeking advice and advice containing various communication approaches. Specific strategies aimed at mitigating serious alcohol-related harm were most commonly reported. Communication content varied by the child’s legal drinking status (under 21 vs. 21 or over), educational background (college vs. non-college), and, to a lesser extent, gender. Consistent with previous research, mothers were more likely than fathers to explicitly discuss protective behavioral strategies and to promote autonomous decision-making, which is an especially relevant strategy targeted at emerging adults who are grappling with instability and identity formation stress. These findings underscore the variation in parental harm-reduction messaging and suggest opportunities to support more effective alcohol safety conversations between parents and emerging adult children.

articles.title: Support Relative to Strain in the College Years: Examining Long-term Mental Health Implications
articles.authors: Carolyn Aldredge, Anne-Chanel Renald, Madeline Brence, Noelle M. Hurd
articles.abstract: We investigated whether levels of social support relative to social strain from key sources (i.e., parents, friends, and natural mentors) during college predicted mental health outcomes in early adulthood among a sample of underrepresented college students attending a predominantly White institution ( N = 340). We compared the more commonly used stress-buffering approach to a novel ratio approach to capture support relative to strain. Results of our path analyses indicated that social support did not buffer the negative impact of social strain on mental health outcomes in early adulthood. In a separate model, the ratio of support to strain during college was negatively associated with depression and loneliness and positively associated with global self-worth, flourishing, and life satisfaction in early adulthood. Creating a ratio of social support relative to social strain may serve as a useful approach to capture the combined impact of support and strain from key relationships on mental health outcomes.

articles.title: Considerations of Military Couples’ Relationship Satisfaction: A Systematic Review
articles.authors: Shulamit Sternin, Alexandra Liepmann, Lisa Weyandt
articles.abstract: Military couples face a unique constellation of stressors that may impact relationship satisfaction, a central indicator of relational stability and individual well-being. Although a substantial body of research has examined mental health symptoms and military-related stressors with respect to relationship functioning, this literature remains conceptually and methodologically heterogeneous. The present systematic review synthesized and critically evaluated empirical studies examining (a) associations between mental health symptoms and relationship satisfaction and (b) associations between adverse military-related events (e.g., deployment, reintegration, combat exposure) and relationship satisfaction among military couples. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, a search across five databases yielded 63 eligible studies. Findings demonstrated consistent negative associations between post-traumatic stress disorder, depressive symptoms, and psychological distress and relationship satisfaction, with effect sizes generally in the small-to-moderate range and stronger effects observed in dyadic and longitudinal designs. Associations between adverse military-related events and relationship satisfaction were more heterogeneous, often varying with communication processes, partner support, caregiving burden, and meaning-making. Across domains, the literature was characterized by variability in construct operationalization, reporting source (service member vs. partner), and methodological rigor, including frequent reliance on cross-sectional designs and limited demographic diversity. These findings underscore the importance of theory-driven, dyadic, and longitudinal research to clarify mechanisms linking mental health and adverse military-related events to relationship satisfaction, informing couple-based interventions targeting both individual and relational processes.

articles.title: If You Follow, Will I Tell You? Associations Between Interpersonal Movement Synchrony, Perceived Closeness, and Expressivity
articles.authors: Alissa von Großmann, Jenny Jaquet, Antje Rauers, Andrea Schlesier-Michel, Elisabeth S. Blanke, Uwe Altmann, Michaela Riediger
articles.abstract: Throughout life, strong social connections foster well-being. Expressing self-relevant information can strengthen these connections. We aim to understand the role of responders’ responsive behavior in promoting speakers’ expressivity and interpersonal closeness by investigating responders’ individual contributions to dyadic movement synchrony. Taking a dyadic perspective, we hypothesized that responders’ motor following (i.e., movement alignment with speakers) is associated with speakers’ perceived closeness and expressivity, and that speakers’ closeness is linked to their own expressivity. We explored interindividual differences with the example of adult age. We analyzed 101 videos of dyadic conversations among unacquainted younger (20–31) and older (69–80) women paired in age-homogeneous or age-heterogeneous dyads. Motor following was assessed via video analyses, expressivity with behavioral coding, and closeness using self-reports. Contrary to our hypotheses, responders’ motor following was not significantly associated with speakers’ perceived closeness or expressivity. However, exploratory analyses considering age as a moderator revealed that among older, but not younger, speakers, responders’ increased motor following was associated with higher perceived closeness. As hypothesized, participants’ higher closeness was linked to their own higher expression of thoughts and feelings. Unexpectedly, participants’ expressivity was linked to their own motor following, suggesting both behaviors reflect conversational engagement. We speculate that older adults may perceive motor following as responsive, possibly indicating age-related differences in social processes.

articles.title: The Political Leaning of Fact-Checking: Countering Italian Disinformation on the War in Ukraine
articles.authors: Tommaso Valastro, Sergio Splendore
articles.abstract: The intense disinformation efforts that accompanied Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine highlight the importance of countering misinformation to mitigate the influence of foreign actors, particularly in vulnerable public spheres such as the Italian one. Despite widespread use, the effectiveness of fact-checking in correcting misinformation remains ambiguous, with limited exploration of the underlying reasons. This article focuses on the role of political leaning and partisanship in shaping individuals’ comprehension of factual information, their inclination to fact-checking exposure, and their capacity to assimilate findings that challenge their preconceived beliefs. We measure the role of these variables for 10 different statements about Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, employing original survey data collected in Italy in spring 2022. We find veracity assessment to be associated with partisan views of the war for both true and false statements, with Russia-leaning views frequently correlating with lower exposure to and reception of fact-checks. Right-leaning political attitudes often work in the same direction, in some cases amplifying the partisan rejection of fact-checks. These findings contribute to literature on fact-checking, selective exposure, motivated reasoning, and misinformation, corroborating previous studies on the limits of debunking efforts and extending their insights to a setting well known for its high level of political parallelism. A crucial implication of these results is that political attitudes should receive greater consideration when addressing misinformation and foreign disinformation efforts, given their potential to amplify partisan barriers that moderate the corrective power of fact-checking. Furthermore, this partisan acceptance of fact-checks complicates the normative assessment of journalistic practices.

articles.title: Counterspeech or Disagreement? Comparing Oppositional Replies in China’s AI Controversies on Social Media
articles.authors: Lishuang Wei, Chuanlin Ning
articles.abstract: Online technological controversies often involve both ordinary disagreement and counterspeech, yet these forms of opposition are rarely compared within the same discussion environment. Drawing on argumentation theories, this study compares disagreement replies to non-hateful comments with counterspeech replies to hateful comments in Douyin discussions of China’s AI controversies, where hate speech may include stigmatizing generalizations about social groups. Using 9,407 oppositional parent–response dyads, we compared like counts, toxicity, subsequent toxic replies, and the distribution and reception of six response types. Counterspeech and disagreement did not differ significantly in like counts, but counterspeech exhibited higher toxicity and was related to greater odds of toxicity among direct replies posted within seven days. Despite sharing the same six response types, the two response contexts varied in their type distributions and associations with likes. These findings situate counterspeech within a broader spectrum of online opposition, revealing contextual differences in its argumentative expression and subsequent interaction across hateful and non-hateful contexts.

articles.title: Digital Fem-Washing of War: Olena Zelenska’s Vogue Cover and the #sitlikeagirl Campaign
articles.authors: Karolina Szpyrko
articles.abstract: This article examines the media controversy surrounding Olena Zelenska’s 2022 <em>Vogue</em> photoshoot, including audience reactions, subsequent news coverage, and the feminist social media campaign #sitlikeagirl. It investigates how feminist discourse became mobilised within highly mediatised wartime communication. Drawing on conjunctural cross-platform analysis of social media posts, Instagram comments, and news coverage, the study reveals a significant discrepancy between dominant journalistic framings of the controversy and the discourse visible within the original comment sections. While media coverage repeatedly framed Zelenska as targeted by misogynistic criticism concerning her allegedly “unfeminine” posture, the analysed comments predominantly criticised the political and aesthetic implications of glamourising war through fashion media. The article argues that the viral feminist framing of the campaign emerged less as a direct response to observable sexism and more as a participatory and affective form of wartime digital communication shaped by platform logics, emotional alignment, and recognisable postfeminist activist aesthetics. Situating the campaign within broader debates on participatory war, misinformation, digital activism, and nation branding, the article proposes the concept of digital fem-washing of war to describe how feminist visibility and activist language become incorporated into the communicative infrastructures of contemporary hypermediated warfare.

articles.title: Beyond Technological Lag: Re-Centering Marginalized Media Markets in Global AI Journalism
articles.authors: Mathias-Felipe De-Lima-Santos, Bruce Mutsvairo
articles.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in journalism has been built largely on evidence from well-resourced newsrooms in Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic nations. This thematic issue focuses on media markets that are marginalized economically, politically, linguistically, or epistemically. Its 17 articles examine newsrooms, journalists, educators, developers, and public discourse across Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Europe, Latin America, BRICS (an international group currently comprising 10 countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates), and the Caribbean. Read together, these studies show that AI adoption at the margins is selective, bounded, and human-gated, shaped by subscription costs, scarce local data, missing newsroom policies, state agendas, and dependence on platforms built elsewhere. Journalists respond with layered boundary work and what contributors call “defensive” forms of governance, protecting verification, judgement, and accountability as human domains. The issue also shows that AI is made meaningful through discourse before it is experienced, as hype, risk narratives, and representations position marginalized societies as recipients rather than co-producers of AI futures. We argue that marginality is relational and that it changes what AI does to journalism. We close with an agenda for comparative, locally grounded, and decolonial research on AI and news.

articles.title: WhatsApp Radio “Post” Spectrum: Conflict, Capture, and the Rethinking of Broadcast Space
articles.authors: Emma Heywood, Modibo Galy Cissé, Mirjam De Bruijn
articles.abstract: Broadcasting has historically been understood as a spectrum-based medium organised through the territorial transmission of radio signals. Yet under conditions of conflict and media capture, the organisational practices associated with broadcasting may increasingly be reproduced through alternative communication infrastructures. This article examines the emergence of WhatsApp radio in conflict-affected Mali, where political pressure, declining media independence, and widespread mobile connectivity have encouraged journalists and audiences to organise the production and circulation of news through encrypted messaging networks. Drawing on long-term digital ethnographic observation of Fulani WhatsApp groups, computational analysis of shared visual material, documentary research, and field engagement with journalists, community members, and WhatsApp administrators, the article addresses two questions: how are organisational practices traditionally associated with broadcasting reproduced through WhatsApp under conditions of conflict and media capture; and what does the emergence of WhatsApp radio reveal about the changing organisation of broadcasting beyond the electromagnetic spectrum? The findings show that, although WhatsApp radio operates through digital messaging infrastructures rather than conventional broadcast transmission, it reproduces key organisational characteristics historically associated with broadcasting, including scheduled news bulletins, editorial gatekeeping, recurring programming, and audience expectation. Comparing these practices with earlier forms of pirate broadcasting and other adaptive responses to communicative constraint, the article argues that WhatsApp radio represents a form of post-spectrum broadcasting in which broadcasting is defined less by transmission technology than by the organisational practices through which public information is produced, curated, and circulated.

articles.title: Cyber-Militia and Digital Coercion: Online Targeting and Militarised Communication in Burkina Faso
articles.authors: Samba Dialimpa Badji, Harouna Drabo
articles.abstract: This article examines the emergence of coordinated pro-regime digital networks in Burkina Faso through the concept of “cyber-militia.” Drawing on a comparative qualitative analysis of 468 Facebook entries collected across three online targeting campaigns, the study explores how actors associated with the Brigade d’intervention rapide de la communication (BIR-C) use digital platforms to amplify hostile narratives, intimidate critics, and delegitimise individuals and organisations perceived as threats to the military regime. Combining qualitative content analysis and process tracing, the article identifies three operational logics of cyber-militia communication: escalation and intimidation, persistence and reputational delegitimisation, and institutional delegitimisation. The findings suggest that cyber-militias function as hybrid formations situated at the intersection of propaganda, participatory digital culture, and coercive state power. The article contributes to scholarship on digital media and conflict by proposing cyber-militia as a new analytical framework for understanding coordinated forms of participatory digital coercion in contemporary conflict environments.

articles.title: TikTok as a Site for Ethno-Political Contestations and Conflict Mediation Among Ethiopian Diaspora
articles.authors: Abdissa Zerai, Gizachew Nemomsa
articles.abstract: This study examines how TikTok has served as a site for both ethno-political contestations and conflict mediation in the context of Ethiopia by focusing on the engagement of the Ethiopian diasporic community on the platform. Informed by the deliberative democratic theoretical framework, it addresses how ethno-political contestations among the diasporic community discursively manifest themselves in the TikTok sphere and how such diasporic community mediates the contestations on the platform. In addressing these, critical discourse analysis was employed on purposively selected TikTok content created from October 2023 to September 2024 across four key thematic areas. The findings indicate that the ethno-political contestations among the diasporic community manifested themselves on the TikTok sphere by juxtaposing exclusionary ethnic identity against inclusive pan-Ethiopian identity. Such contestations were enacted through the deployment of charged rhetoric. However, the contestations were mediated by pushing back against destructive discursive trends through strategic intervention of some TikTok hosts. The platform served as a site for both an ideological battlefield and a counter-platform for challenging polemical discourses and for promoting deliberative discourse among the Ethiopian diaspora. Contrary to the prevailing skepticism about TikTok’s potential for meaningful discourse, this study reveals that if deployed strategically, it can be a valuable platform for advancing rational dialogue among disparate groups, which could be instrumental in encouraging participants to seek collective solutions for enduring political problems.

articles.title: Grande Dame of Antifascism: Visual Activism and Unruly Aging of the OMAS GEGEN RECHTS
articles.authors: Ricarda Drüeke, Tanja Maier
articles.abstract: The article analyzes the visual activism of OMAS GEGEN RECHTS (“Grannies against the right”), a movement founded in Austria in 2017 by older feminist women mobilizing against far-right politics. The movement increasingly extends into digital spaces, where political conflict over democratic values and public legitimacy is negotiated. At the same time, forms of protest by older activists remain largely unexplored. Drawing on concepts of agonistic publics, visual activism, and unruliness, we analyze how OMAS GEGEN RECHTS engage with digital media to articulate political positions and intervene in right-wing politics. The study is based on a qualitative analysis of visual practices in Instagram posts published in 2025, focusing on the nationwide account representing Austria: @omasgegenrechts (137K followers in late December 2025). We examine how visual practices are used to mobilize supporters, construct collective identities, and contest right-wing narratives. Our findings reveal how images and symbolic self-representation are used to counter ageist exclusions from digital spaces while simultaneously mobilizing both members of the movement and broader publics. Rather than being marginalized by digital divides, OMAS GEGEN RECHTS actively negotiate platform constraints and transform age into a source of political legitimacy and moral authority. By emphasizing age and visibility as central dimensions of digital conflict, this article contributes to debates on digital media, activism, and political struggles.

articles.title: The science of beauty: Looksmaxxing, self-help, and genetic fatalism in women’s online spaces
articles.authors: Rachel Bergmann, Elizabeth Fetterolf
articles.abstract: This paper examines the emergence of “looksmaxxing” in women’s online spaces. As a specific and underexamined element within what Jilly Boyce Kay analyzes as “reactionary feminism,” essentialist logics about gender and race are operationalized through the aesthetics of science and self-optimization rather than explicitly political rhetoric. Users construct the “science of beauty” through decentralized forms of expertise, from plastic surgery influencers to scientific racism to community-generated aesthetic taxonomies. We identify a thread of individualized and intimate genetic fatalism shaping both aesthetic frameworks and the tactics used to achieve them, mutating the postfeminist promise of self-transformation toward distinctly reactionary goals. This tension between the essentialism and malleability of the body makes the paradigm generative and self-sustaining, absorbing failure and keeping users invested. This case is a call to examine “fringe” and aesthetics-focused cultural formations for insight on how bioessentialist ideas about race and gender circulate today.

articles.title: When availability is not enough: Content prominence and diversity on a public service VoD platform
articles.authors: Raul Lobanov
articles.abstract: As public service media (PSM) shift from broadcasting to video on demand (VoD), prominence has become a key mechanism through which public value is operationalised. While policy debates emphasise the visibility of culturally significant content, evidence on how interface prominence shapes viewing remains scarce. Building on theories of affordances, prominence, and media diversity, this article conceptualises diversity transformation as the process through which diversity changes from catalogue availability, through interface prominence, to audience consumption. Using a longitudinal dataset from Estonian Public Broadcasting (ERR), the study finds that prominence and premieres are the strongest predictors of VoD viewing, explaining 62 per cent of the variance. The findings illustrate a process of diversity transformation: Although ERR’s VoD catalogue is diverse, interface prominence and audience consumption become concentrated around scripted and foreign titles. The study confirms that the VoD interface has become a strategic site where PSM negotiate tensions between universality, cultural responsibility, and audience demand.

articles.title: The Associations Between Depressive Symptoms, Excessive Reassurance‐Seeking, and the Quality of Romantic Relationships in Young Adult Couples: A Dyadic Longitudinal Mediation Model
articles.authors: Fatmawati Fadli, Nicholas J. Moberly, Lamprini Psychogiou
articles.abstract: This study used a dyadic mediation model to examine actor and partner effects in the associations between depressive symptoms and the quality of romantic relationships, both directly and indirectly via excessive reassurance‐seeking. A total of 105 heterosexual young adult couples participated in a three‐wave longitudinal study (waves 1‐month apart) through the Prolific platform. Participants completed measures of depressive symptoms, excessive reassurance‐seeking, and multiple dimensions of romantic relationship qualities at each time point. After controlling for autoregressive and reciprocal effects, several direct and indirect actor and partner effects emerged. Direct actor effects were only significant for men (not women), showing that when men reported higher depressive symptoms at Time 1, they experienced greater companionship, intimate disclosure, and emotional support at Time 3. Direct partner effects were significant for both women and men, indicating that when women reported higher depressive symptoms at Time 1, their partners experienced less companionship and satisfaction at Time 3. However, when men reported higher depressive symptoms at Time 1, their partners reported receiving less criticism at Time 3. In terms of indirect effects, depressive symptoms in men at Time 1 predicted their higher reassurance‐seeking at Time 2, which, in turn, predicted increased partners' perceptions of being criticized and excluded at Time 3 (actor–partner effects). Conversely, depressive symptoms in women at Time 1 predicted higher partners' reassurance‐seeking at Time 2, which, in turn, predicted decreased women's perceptions of being criticized and excluded at Time 3 (partner–partner effects). These findings highlight the complex interpersonal dynamics of depressive symptoms in young adult romantic relationships and suggest that men's excessive reassurance‐seeking may be one potential pathway linking individuals' depressive symptoms with their own and their partners' perceptions and behaviors within romantic relationships.

articles.title: Joke's On You: A Social Relations Analysis of Humor Styles in Friendships
articles.authors: Irene J. Kim, Lily Unger, Hyewon Yang, Mariah F. Purol, William J. Chopik
articles.abstract: Humor plays an important role in the formation and maintenance of close relationships, yet little is known about how people come to perceive their friends as funny or as using different humor styles. The present study examined perceptions of funniness and humor styles in 185 naturally occurring friendship groups ( N = 740). In the context of the Social Relations Model, friends demonstrated modest consensus regarding humor styles and funniness, indicating that humor is sufficiently observable to generate shared impressions. At the same time, substantial perceiver and relationship variances suggested that humor judgments are also shaped by individual tendencies and the unique dynamics of particular friendships. Self‐other agreement and assumed similarity were also evident across humor styles. Finally, adaptive humor styles and general funniness were associated with greater friendship satisfaction, while aggressive and self‐defeating humor were associated with poorer friendship quality. These findings position humor as both an individual characteristic and an interpersonal perception that emerges through close relationships.

articles.title: From Anger to Contempt: The Emotional Pathways to Satisfaction Loss and Divorce in Romantic Relationships
articles.authors: Inmaculada Valor‐Segura, Agneta Fischer, María Alonso‐Ferres, Bertjan Doojse
articles.abstract: Having a satisfying intimate relationship is a key predictor of happiness and emotional well‐being, yet conflict is an inevitable aspect of romantic life. Different emotions play a central role in shaping how partners experience and manage conflict and may have distinct relational consequences. The present research includes three studies examining the differential roles of anger and contempt in romantic conflict. Drawing on prior work suggesting that anger may serve adaptive functions whereas contempt is more destructive, we investigated their motivational, behavioral, and relational implications. In Study 1 ( N = 276), participants recalled a conflict in which they felt either anger or contempt toward their partner. Anger was associated with verbal attack and coercion, which in turn were weakly and positively associated with relationship satisfaction, whereas contempt was linked to partner derogation and social exclusion, which were associated with lower satisfaction. Study 2 ( N = 363) replicated these findings across diverse conflict types, showing that anger was mainly associated with verbal attack and coercion goals but not with divorce intentions, whereas past and current contempt were associated with partner derogation, social exclusion, lower relationship quality, and stronger divorce intentions. Study 3 experimentally induced romantic conflict in 60 couples. Severe conflicts uniquely amplified contempt—but not anger—and post‐conflict contempt was strongly predicted by pre‐existing levels of anger and contempt, suggesting that contempt responses may reflect accumulated emotional dispositions rather than reactions to the conflict at hand. Together, these findings underscore the importance of distinguishing discrete negative emotions in romantic conflict and highlight the particularly harmful role of contempt in relationship deterioration.

articles.title: Navigating Infertility Together: The Influence of Romantic Attachment on Couple Outcomes—A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
articles.authors: Camilla Tacchino, Rosetta Castellano, Guyonne Rogier, Teresa Cocchiaro, Alessandro Dal Lago, Rocco Rago, Patrizia Velotti
articles.abstract: Infertility is a significant public health concern, profoundly affecting both individuals and couples. This systematic review and meta‐analysis aims to explore whether romantic attachment serves as a protective or risk factor in how couples navigate infertility diagnoses, treatments, and outcomes, with a specific focus on relational correlates. A systematic search was conducted across six databases from January 1, 2011, to February 3, 2025. Seventeen studies met the inclusion criteria, examining the link between romantic attachment and couple‐related psychological outcomes. Five of these studies were included in a meta‐analysis assessing the associations between attachment anxiety and avoidance and dyadic adjustment. Findings highlight significant associations between insecure attachment dimensions (both anxiety and avoidance) and reduced relationship and sexual satisfaction among individuals facing infertility. Meta‐analytic results revealed moderate negative associations between attachment insecurities and dyadic adjustment. Additionally, cross‐partner effects were observed, indicating that one partner's attachment style can impact the other's infertility experience. This study underscores the pivotal role of romantic attachment in managing infertility‐related challenges, distinguishing the distinct impacts of attachment anxiety and avoidance, and offering valuable clinical insights for supporting couples undergoing fertility treatments.

articles.title: When I See You Smile: Links Among Experienced Affect, Expressed Emotional Components, and Target Readability in a Supportive Interaction
articles.authors: Alexandrija Zikic, Michele Morningstar, Erin P. Macdonald, Laurence Jette, Lauren J. Human, Jennifer A. Bartz, Melanie A. Dirks
articles.abstract: Navigating supportive interactions is an important task of friendship that involves exchanging affective information. However, experienced affect is not always readable, and emotional expressions are not all equally helpful in conveying experienced affect. We examined associations between target readability (i.e., emotional expressive accuracy, or the degree to which individuals accurately communicate their experienced affect to others), and experienced and expressed emotional components (i.e., facial expressions and affect words), when seeking support from a friend. Participants ( N = 137 dyads, M age = 19.61 years, SD age = 1.34 years) took turns discussing problems they were having. To measure experienced affect, participants reported their positive and negative affect during the interaction. Expressed emotional components were participants' facial movements (i.e., eyebrow movements and smiles) and use of positive and negative affect words. To measure readability, observers continuously rated participants' affect during the interaction; their ratings were correlated with similar self‐ratings made by participants, and those correlations were averaged. Participants were more readable when they reported experiencing greater negative affect. In terms of expressed emotional components, participants were more readable when they had more eyebrow raises, and fewer eyebrow furrows and smiles. Results elucidate factors that contribute to effective communication of experienced affect when seeking support from friends.

articles.title: Fandom Rupture in the Movement Society: Reactive Collective Participation Through Affective Practices
articles.authors: Zhihong Li
articles.abstract: When an external shock draws heterogeneous actors into a single platform arena before any collective aim emerges, participation persists at movement-like intensity. Existing theories have not specified the cohering mechanism through which this formation sustains. This study conceptualizes this mode as reactive collective participation and specifies how affective publics cohere and persist under reactive conditions at the practice level. A mixed-methods design integrates in-depth interviews with 13 heterogeneously positioned participants (fans, anti-fans, bystanders) and computational analysis of Weibo discourse surrounding the 2023 Cai Xukun scandal (139,795 posts; 205,001 comments). Four affective practices recur across the event: Positioning, Storying, Attunement, and Calibration. These practices shift in relative weight across the event’s life cycle and distribute unevenly across actor positions, producing a stratified ecology in which insulated defense and exposed antagonism sustain each other. The study advances affective publics theory by specifying how affective publics cohere and persist under reactive conditions at practice level, and collective participation theory by conceptualizing reactive collective participation as a mode that reconnects the movement society and fan activism frameworks through a reactive pathway.

articles.title: Women Sustaining TikTok as Supplementary Information Infrastructure for Flexible Work Arrangements: Gendered Conditions, Community and Surveillance
articles.authors: Xuefei Li, Kiran Ijaz, Marta E. Cecchinato, Naseem Ahmadpour
articles.abstract: Flexible work arrangements (FWAs) create practical and interpretive questions that formal workplace information may not adequately address, particularly around how flexibility is experienced and negotiated in everyday working life. As workers share and encounter FWA-related posts on TikTok, the platform can provide supplementary access to experiential knowledge. However, circulation alone does not explain how such knowledge becomes a durable and usable resource for workers. Drawing on infrastructure theory, we conceptualise TikTok as a supplementary information infrastructure (SII) and use a feminist perspective to examine the gendered conditions under which women contribute to and sustain it. Based on semi-structured interviews with 14 women who post about FWAs on TikTok, we analyse their relational information practices. Participants responded to misleading information with situated knowledge and interpretive resources that made workplace norms more visible and contestable. Sustaining this infrastructure came at a cost: credibility and continued participation were shaped by gendered conditions of recognition and unequal access to time and energy, while trust was challenged by shifting audiences, limited contextualisation and technological risks. Participation also exposed women creators to workplace-facing surveillance. We contribute an infrastructural account of digital workplace knowledge exchange by showing how creators’ repair and maintenance labour helps sustain TikTok as an SII. This extends research on digital workplace knowledge exchange by showing that supplementary workplace knowledge can also matter for workers who remain connected to formal workplace information. The SII’s possibilities for information justice nevertheless remain uneven because they depend on creator labour undertaken under gendered and platformed conditions.
